## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The Buddha explains that terror and dread afflict recluses who retreat into seclusion while harboring unpurified bodily, verbal, or mental conduct, or corrupt livelihood [Stanley et al. 2018]. By contrast, having established rigorous moral purity and continuous mindfulness, one remains undisturbed by internal anxiety and external disturbances in the forest, such as the sudden cracking of branches or animal movements [Stanley et al. 2018; Anālayo 2017]. The cultivation of friendliness (*mettā*) is also presented as a characteristic quality of noble practitioners (*ariya*) that grants confidence in wilderness living [Gaffney 2003].

The text is renowned for its autobiographical narrative of the Buddha's quest for awakening [Segall 2003; Anderson 1999]. Recounting his practice before bodhi, the Buddha describes ascending through the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and attaining the three higher knowledges (*tevijjā*) during the three watches of the night: the recollection of past lives, the divine eye discerning the rebirth of beings according to their karma, and the knowledge of the destruction of the influxes (*āsava*) aligned with the four noble truths [Appleton 2014; Cantwell 2010; Anderson 1999; Shulman 2014].

DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse (3,517 matches across 154 texts), with major verbatim sharing occurring across the Aṅguttara Nikāya (AN 10, AN 5, AN 4, AN 3, AN 8), the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (Pārājika 1), and discourses such as DN 2, DN 25, MN 19, and MN 85 [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language machine alignments connect sections of the sutta with the Sanskrit *Daśabalasūtra* and *Catuṣpariṣatsūtra*, the Tibetan *Vinayavastu*, and Chinese Āgama texts [DharmaNexus].
